content: HAX1, also known as HCLS1-associated protein X-1, is a protein encoded by the HAX1 gene in humans. This protein is known to associate with HS1, which is a substrate of Src family tyrosine kinases. Additionally, HAX1 interacts with the product of the PKD2 gene, mutations in which are linked to autosomal-dominant polycystic kidney disease. It also binds to cortactin, a protein that interacts with filamentous actin (F-actin). Initially, it was believed that the HAX1 protein was predominantly localized in the mitochondria. However, more recent studies have demonstrated that it is primarily localized in the cell body. Two transcript variants of the HAX1 gene have been identified, each encoding different isoforms of the protein. In 2015, it was further shown that the HAX1 protein is localized to P-bodies, which are cytoplasmic structures involved in mRNA regulation and decay. Homozygous mutations in the HAX1 gene are associated with autosomal recessive severe congenital neutropenia, also referred to as Kostmann syndrome. This condition is characterized by a profound deficiency of neutrophils, a type of white blood cell essential for fighting infections. HAX1 has been shown to interact with interleukin-1 alpha (IL1A). Furthermore, it has been demonstrated to bind to the 3' untranslated regions (UTRs) of vimentin and DNA polymerase beta transcripts, suggesting a role in post-transcriptional regulation of these genes.
